- opened gap-001 [partial] spec:"edge case: a description mentions a neighbouring property's
  feature, or a feature of a nearby development. Attribution to the subject property is required,
  which is what AC-13 exists to enforce"

  Evidence: `extract/model.py` `_one`, which checks that a model's quote appears in the description,
  and `extract/model.py` `instruction`, which tells the model that a neighbour's feature is not this
  property's. `extract/patterns.py` has nothing for it at all.

  What is enforced is attribution to **the text**, which is what AC-13 says in its own words and
  what the quote check delivers exactly. What the edge case asks for is attribution to **the subject
  property**, which is a different and harder claim: "the neighbour has a well" is in the text, and a
  verbatim quote proves it is in the text, and it is still not a fact about the house for sale.

  For the model this is an instruction rather than a check, which is the weaker of the two defences
  this feature uses everywhere else. For the deterministic patterns it is nothing: a sentence
  attributing a septic system to the property next door would be read as this property's.

  Why it is not remediated here: it does not occur. Zero of the 263 descriptions in the committed
  corpus contain a sentence mentioning a neighbour, an adjacent property or a nearby development
  together with any utility word. The construction real prose actually uses is the opposite one:
  the neighbourhood is described as an amenity (`a nearby and well kept country store`), never as
  the owner of a utility. Building a subject-attribution check against zero examples would be
  building it against a guess, which is what this feature's whole design is against.

  Routed: recorded, not remediated. If a corpus ever contains one, the shape of the fix is a
  disqualifier in the same window `_A_PROSPECT` already reads, and the entry to add is a
  possessive-neighbour phrase. Recorded so the first person to see a wrong value here starts from
  the right place.

- opened gap-002 [partial] spec:"edge case: the same property is described differently by two
  sources. Each description is extracted independently and the canonical listing carries both, with
  conflicts visible rather than resolved by preference order"

  Evidence: `extract/__init__.py` `values_for`, which reads one description, and `plan.md` D-14,
  which says why and what the other path would be.

  What is missing is not the code. **Only one of the three shipped sources returns a description at
  all.** Zillow's search response has no description field and Redfin's CSV has no description
  column, which was measured by reading all three normalization modules and confirmed against 1,231
  live rows: 1,176 carried prose and every one of them came from Realtor.com. A canonical listing
  therefore never has two descriptions to disagree about.

  The conflict machinery this edge case wants is built and is exercised, just one level down: two
  statements inside *one* description leave the field empty with both sentences kept
  (`extract/__init__.py` `_from_patterns`, tested against a real corpus sentence and observed twice
  in a live run over Portales). Extending it across sources is a loop over `store.source_links` and
  nothing else, which D-14 writes down.

  Routed: no remediation task, because there is nothing this feature can build that any source can
  exercise. Reopens by itself the day an adapter starts returning prose.

- opened gap-003 [unrequested] code:"`homescout extract --limit N`"

  Evidence: `cli/main.py` `build_parser`, `api.extract`, `extract/pass_.py` `run_pass`.

  A bound on how many descriptions one pass will ask about, which the spec never asks for. It exists
  because a first pass over a county with the model on is thousands of paced requests, and a person
  trying the feature out should be able to spend ten of them rather than all of them.

  It is off unless asked for, it is never a default, and what it leaves behind is named in the
  outcome and printed, so it cannot become a silent truncation. That last part is the reason it is
  worth keeping rather than removing: a cap nobody reports would read as a market where nobody
  mentions a septic tank, and this is the version that says so.

  Routed: a human decision. The recommendation is to legitimize it as an addition to AC-6 rather
  than remove it. Recorded, not self-applied.

## What was checked and found clean

- **The patterns were built against real prose and are tested against it.** 1,231 live listings were
  pulled before anything was designed, 1,176 of them carrying a description, and the two
  measurements that shaped the design are in `plan.md`: roughly one occurrence of `well` in seven is
  about water, and roughly three utility mentions in ten are hedged, negated or prospective rather
  than an assertion. 263 of those descriptions are committed as the fixture, with the prose kept
  verbatim and every price, address, telephone number, listing number, URL and agent name replaced.
  A test asserts that last part rather than trusting the script that did it.
- **Precision is asserted at the scale the traps occur.** `well-maintained` is checked across every
  description in the corpus that contains it, not once; so is every hedged utility sentence, and so
  is `new roof`, which outnumbers `metal roof` in real listings and says nothing about a material.
- **Product invariant 10 survives contact with a language model.** Three separate mechanisms, and
  the weakest of them is the prompt: a value must be a member of a closed vocabulary declared in
  this repository, it must arrive with a quote, and the quote must be in the description. A test
  drives a model that obeys an injection and asserts that obeying it achieves nothing.
- **Product invariant 9 is proved hostilely rather than asserted.** Every extraction variable is
  removed from the environment, the whole tool is run end to end, and the six fields still fill from
  prose with no key, no address and no network. A transport that raises on contact stands in for the
  network so "nothing was contacted" is proved by nothing being able to.
- **Only the description leaves the machine.** The request is built by a function that is handed
  prose and a list of field names and has no access to a listing, and a test serializes the body of
  a request built from a property with a known address, price, coordinates, link and identifier and
  asserts the body contains none of them. This was the pre-build check's hard finding against the
  first draft of the plan, which described the request shape and never said what went in it.
- **A run degrades rather than fails.** A model that cannot be reached costs the fields it would
  have filled: the deterministic values stand because they never involved a network, the affected
  fields stay empty rather than being filled by a fallback, the run finishes and reports itself
  degraded, and a failure is not cached as an answer while an answered nothing is.
- **The cache is keyed by the words rather than by the property.** Three listings sharing one
  description are one request; the same description on a hundred nights is one request; and the
  model is part of the key, so a person who changes models can ask again. A test closes and reopens
  the database to prove the cache is in it rather than in an object that dies with the run.
- **A silent listing never excludes a house.** Verified on a live run over Portales: of 83
  properties, a `water_source == "well"` criterion fired on 2, was false for 2, and was undetermined
  for 79. Undetermined is not false, so nothing was dropped for want of a description.
- **Two statements about one field is not a value, and a person can see why.** Observed twice in
  that same live run, and `homescout extract --listing` shows both sentences.
